summary: Digital mental health interventions show promise but have yet to meet expectations. We discuss gaps between promising results of pilot studies and null findings in randomized controlled trials, focusing on two major approaches: just-in-time relapse prevention and just-in-time adaptive interventions. We propose that relapse prevention will profit from long-term studies capturing emerging episodes, and we suggest a novel framework for adaptive interventions including causality testing to proceed towards effective trialing.
title: Effective trialing of digital interventions in daily life – the mental health perspective

summary: Affordable electroencephalography (EEG) headsets could widen access to EEG-based treatment and assessment, but require rigorous validation. We evaluated PainWaive, a custom-developed 2-channel central scalp EEG headset designed for remote EEG monitoring and neurofeedback research in chronic pain. Eighty participants completed two resting-state EEGs using PainWaive and a research-grade system (LiveAmp). Alpha, beta and theta power, and peak alpha frequency (PAF), were derived from homologous central channels. PainWaive demonstrated good-to-excellent test-retest reliability for alpha power and PAF (ICCs = 0.72–0.93), with beta and theta ranging from moderate-good (ICCs = 0.42–0.76). Across 160 home-based neurofeedback sessions in two chronic pain samples, reliability was good-to-excellent across metrics (ICCs = 0.72–0.88). Spectral-shape correlations between PainWaive and LiveAmp were excellent (r > 0.91). Cross-device agreement was moderate-to-good for alpha power and PAF (ICCs = 0.53–0.74), but weaker for beta and theta (ICCs = 0.16–0.51). Sensitivity analyses showed alpha power and PAF were robust across choices, whereas beta and theta agreement varied by pipeline. Overall, PainWaive demonstrated reliable measurement of central scalp EEG metrics, supporting repeated within-device monitoring. Cross-device findings showed correspondence with research-grade EEG for some measures but should not be interpreted as establishing direct numerical interchangeability between systems. These findings provide a technical foundation for future remote EEG and neurofeedback studies in chronic pain.
title: Evaluation of PainWaive: a consumer-grade EEG headset for remote EEG monitoring and neurofeedback research in chronic pain

summary: Online medicine sales have not only improved access but also expose consumers to illegal online medicine vendors (IOMVs) selling substandard/falsified products. This study provides the first pan-European assessment of exposure to legitimate online pharmacies (LOPs) and IOMVs in search engine results (SERs). We scraped the top-50 Google results in 30 European countries for six tracer active pharmaceutical ingredients across three categories: controlled substances, prescription-only medicines (POMs), and over-the-counter products (OTCs). Links were categorised as LOPs or IOMVs based on official registries. From 9000 SERs, 3839 linked to medicine-selling websites (63.7% LOPs, 36.3% IOMVs). LOPs outnumbered and outranked IOMVs, though IOMV:LOP ratios reached 2.37 (Norway) and 2.18 (Cyprus). Search engine redirection affected 56.6% of IOMV links. IOMV prevalence increased with regulatory control: 1.4% (paracetamol), 5.5% (ibuprofen), 10.2% (omeprazole), 55.1% (amoxicillin), 76.2% (alprazolam) and 77.5% (clonazepam). IOMV links were less likely to be highest-ranked and less common in the top-10 SERs in countries permitting online OTC and POM sales, than in those prohibiting them. Despite LOP dominance, Europeans face substantial exposure to IOMV links, higher for controlled substances and in countries prohibiting online sales. Harmonised regulatory action, supported by search engine providers, is needed for safer online medication access.
title: Exposure to legitimate and illegal online medicine vendors via search engines in 30 European countries

summary: Safe deprioritization of non-contrast brain computed tomography (NCCT) demands high sensitivity and negative predictive value (NPV) across common and uncommon findings requiring clinical attention. Here, we present a collaborative safety net integrating BrainCT-CLIP, a generalist foundation model via contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP), with commercial detectors. Every examination remained in the reporting workflow, deprioritized only when no model returned a positive result. In a retrospective multicenter external validation of consecutive emergency and trauma cohorts (n = 2001), standalone commercial detectors left 31 of 324 remarkable examinations deprioritized, including 16 target-disease false negatives and 15 outside their indications. In contrast, the collaborative system recovered every remarkable examination at a threshold prespecified in the development cohort, achieving 100% sensitivity and NPV while deprioritizing 18% of examinations (368/2001; 95% CI, 17–20). These findings support generalist-specialist AI for safe worklist deprioritization under radiologist oversight, with high sensitivity for intracranial findings requiring clinical attention.
title: Collaborative generalist-specialist AI for safe worklist deprioritization of non-contrast brain computed tomography

summary: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) complicated by unstable angina (UA) represents a major challenge in chronic disease management with high risk of recurrent heart failure hospitalization (HFH), and despite the availability of multicenter real-world data, AI-driven tools for multi-horizon risk assessment remain limited. This multicenter retrospective cohort enrolled 4367 patients with UA and HFpEF, and an ensemble feature selection pipeline integrating LASSO, SVM-RFE and Boruta identified robust predictors, followed by training of twelve machine learning algorithms to estimate HFH risk at 12-, 24- and 36-month horizons with external validation. The optimal time-specific models (ET, GBDT and LightGBM) achieved strong discrimination in the training cohort with AUCs of 0.818, 0.834 and 0.863, and maintained performance in external validation with AUCs of 0.839, 0.836 and 0.851, respectively, while SHAP analysis highlighted diabetes mellitus, TyG-BMI and NT-proBNP as the most influential predictors. We developed and externally validated a multi-time-point machine learning framework for HFH risk stratification in UA and HFpEF, which showed acceptable calibration and potential clinical utility on decision-curve analysis. Further prospective and real-world validation across diverse populations and healthcare systems is needed to confirm clinical effectiveness and support translation into routine practice.
title: AI-driven multi-horizon risk stratification for heart failure hospitalization in UA with HFpEF: a Chinese multi-center cohort study

summary: Pregnancy dating fails the women who need it most: those who reach care without a first-trimester scan. We externally validated a commercial image-only ultrasound deep-learning model for delivery-date prediction, applied unmodified to 64,235 frames from 3788 examinations of 2550 pregnancies (34% migrant) at four Chilean public hospitals. Mean absolute error was 6.9 days versus 11.6 for the conventional due date, yet most of this gain reflected a shorter local gestation and fell below one day against recentred comparators. Fixed-term comparators assign every pregnancy the same gestational age at birth and therefore cannot rank who will deliver early, at any level of point accuracy: accuracy metrics are blind to the ranking on which management turns whenever the outcome distribution is concentrated, as in term-dominated cohorts. In a prespecified landmark analysis the model’s separate image-only risk score discriminated preterm birth with an area under the curve of 0.86, against 0.52 for gestational age alone; outside the landmark restriction it exceeded a clinical baseline of coded diagnoses plus same-examination biometry by 0.09, although it was miscalibrated. Error and calibration were also assessed by maternal nationality. These classification analyses are exploratory, and no woman was managed with the model; they identify what a prospective study should test.
title: External validation of an image-only ultrasound model for delivery-date prediction in four Chilean public hospitals

summary: Digital and hybrid interventions combining exercise, education, and psychological components are increasingly used for low back pain (LBP), but it remains unclear which components and combinations drive efficacy. We conducted a prospectively registered component network meta-analysis (CNMA) to evaluate their efficacy and safety for non-specific LBP. Six databases and two trial registries were searched to May 2025. Data on disability, pain intensity, and adverse events were analysed using a Bayesian random-effects CNMA. Of 2809 records, 56 reports of 46 studies (6717 participants; 80% chronic low back pain) were included. Hybrid interventions combining digital and in-person exercise with in-person psychological components (MD: –22.21; 95%-CrI: –34.11 to –10.67), digital and in-person exercise (MD: –15.75; 95%-CrI: –22.79 to –8.80), or digital exercise with physiotherapy (MD: –13.17; 95%-CrI: –21.18 to –5.16) reduced disability versus no intervention at short-term (minimal clinically important difference (MCID): 4.92/100 Oswestry Disability Index). Digital and in-person exercise (MD: -1.76; 95%-CrI: -2.62; -0.87) and combined digital exercise training with in-person education (MD: -1.73; 95%-CrI: -2.71; -0.83) improved pain intensity beyond the MCID (0.82/10 numeric pain rating scale). No serious adverse events were noted. Multicomponent hybrid interventions appear safe and may provide clinically meaningful improvements for chronic LBP.
title: Digital and hybrid interventions for subacute and chronic low back pain: component network meta-analysis

summary: Large language models are increasingly being used to evaluate clinical texts, a concept known as LLM-as-a-judge. However, most of the existing evidence focuses on English data and uses pooled agreement metrics that obscure clinically relevant failure modes. This study audited six open-weight models against expert judges on four German clinical datasets covering report and nursing documentation summarization, discharge summary generation, and patient letter generation. The models were evaluated across three paradigms and four prompt configurations. Alignment with experts varied by criterion and corpus, and no configuration proved reliable across paradigms. All judges exhibited position and identity bias. Substituting LLM-as-a-judge for the expert panel shifted 57.2% of pointwise categories, swapped 41.7% of pairwise winners, missed 10.2% of clinical errors, and inverted clinical priorities by overrating the criteria succinct and accurate. Therefore, LLM-as-a-judge is not a safe substitute for experts in German clinical text evaluations, and deployment thresholds should follow decision-impact analysis for LLM-as-a-judge in clinical contexts.
title: Cross-paradigm audit of large language model judges for clinical text evaluation
